1:
The title says a prayer of David, and two of them doubt it. Adam Clarke grants that all the versions agree with the title, but observes that in structure the psalm is the same as those ascribed to the sons of Korah and was probably made during the captivity. Keil and Delitzsch go further, and their reason is aesthetic: it can be called a psalm by David only as having grown out of Davidic and other model passages, since the writer cannot be compared for poetical capability either with David or with the authors of two other psalms they name, his work being more liturgic than purely poetic. They support this with a catalogue, that almost everything here is an echo of earlier language in the Psalms and the Law, and they trace half a dozen verses to their sources. John Calvin keeps David and refers the psalm to the persecution by Saul, while allowing that it may not have been written until after his restoration to outward peace, when he had greater leisure. Matthew Henry notices exactly the quality that Keil and Delitzsch count against the poem and counts it in its favour: it is observable how very plain the language is, and how little there is of poetic flights or figures compared with other psalms, since the flourishes of wit are not the proper ornaments of prayer.

The claim in the second verse is the hardest thing here, and it is met four ways. Clarke removes the difficulty by translating the word actively, for I am merciful, and gives the sense of the whole prayer in a couplet asking that the mercy he shows to others be shown to him. Charles Ellicott keeps the passive sense but changes its ground, rendering it as one of the chosen ones, one of thy saints, so that what is pleaded is the covenant relation rather than a character. John Wesley narrows it to devotion, sincerely devoted to thy service. John Gill passes over the word and applies the petition itself to Christ, whose life was preserved in infancy and in the wilderness and from those who sought it before his time.

On the opening request they agree in one thing, that it asks God to stoop. Clarke states the reason plainly, that the petitioner is so low and so weak that unless God bends his voice cannot reach. Henry says it is admirable condescension that he takes notice of such creatures and such defective prayers, and that the whole psalm is prayer proper, since though prayer may accidentally preach, it is most fit that every passage be directed to God. C.H. Spurgeon finds the argument in the weakness itself, that misery is ever the master argument with mercy, and then turns on those who borrow the words without the condition: such reasoning would never be adopted by a proud man, and when it is repeated in public worship by great ones of the earth who count the peasantry little better than the ground they tread on, it sounds like a mockery. Calvin makes the same point as doctrine, that nothing is more suitable to the nature of God than to succour the afflicted, and the more destitute a man is of human aid the more inclined God is to help him. Augustine of Hippo resolves the speaker instead, in a formula: Christ prays for us as our priest, prays in us as our head, and is prayed to by us as our God.
5:
Where the argument turns is noticed by Charles Ellicott. Up to this point the psalmist has only put forward his needs in various aspects as a plea for compassion; now, not without art, he clenches the petition by appealing to the nature of God himself, and the expressions he uses are drawn from the older revelations of that nature. Ellicott then dwells on the word rendered ready to forgive, which occurs nowhere else in this form and etymologically means remitting; the Greek version renders it by a term for which our word considerate is perhaps the nearest equivalent, implying that legal right is overlooked and suspended in consideration of human weakness. Adam Clarke rests the same verse on two grounds at once, God’s own goodness and his well-known character, to which all his followers bear testimony. John Gill distinguishes the kinds of goodness meant, essential and independent in himself, providential toward all, and gracious toward his own.

The renewed request that follows is read as a fresh beginning. Ellicott says simply that the petition here takes a new starting-point. Gill notes that the psalmist calls this his own prayer, not one composed for him but by him, and that the repetition shows importunity. Clarke turns the repetition into evidence of earnestness and counts three marks of it: that he prayed, that his prayer was vehement and he lifted up his voice, and that he continued in prayer and abounded in supplications. He also puts the plea in its bluntest form, that millions call for help and mercy but none has more need than himself.

On the day of trouble Gill supplies an anatomy of where trouble comes from. Some of it rises from the sufferers themselves, from their corruptions, the weakness of their grace and the poor performance of their duties; some from others, from persecution, from the wicked lives of profane sinners and especially of professors of religion, and from the spread of false doctrine; some from Satan and his temptations; and some from the more immediate hand of God in afflictions and in the hiding of his face. His comfort is that such troubles do not last always but are for a day, and that such a season is a fit one for prayer. Clarke grounds the confidence of being answered in the character just confessed. Keil and Delitzsch place the speaker rather than the doctrine, finding the situation like that of the psalms belonging to the time of Saul, the writer being a persecuted man in constant peril of his life.
8:
The gods among whom none is like him are identified almost identically by three of them. John Gill offers the angels, on the authority of an Aramaic paraphrase, or civil magistrates, over whom God presides and whom he sets up and puts down at pleasure, or the nominal and fictitious gods of the Gentiles. Matthew Henry lists the same three, the false gods whom the heathens worshipped, the angels, and the kings of the earth. C.H. Spurgeon divides them into gods by delegated office, such as kings and magistrates, and gods by the nomination of superstition, which are vanity itself; then he pushes the comparison past its limit with a supposition of his own, that if every imaginary deity could start into actual existence and become really divine, he would still choose this God and reject all the others. Adam Clarke applies a practical test instead: none who trusted in an idol ever had help in time of need, and none who prayed to one ever had an answer. Charles Ellicott notes only that the psalmist, having expressed his conviction of God’s willingness to hear, now passes to his confidence in the power to save.

On the nations who will come and worship, the question is when. Henry allows a partial fulfilment already, in the multitude of proselytes to the Jewish religion in the days of David and of Solomon, but holds the full accomplishment reserved for the days of the Messiah, when some out of every kingdom should be brought in. Clarke makes it flatly a prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles to the faith of Christ, with the miracles worked as the evidence of his divine mission. Spurgeon grounds the universality in creation, since all mankind come of the first man and each life is a distinct creation. Gill draws the same conclusion as power rather than obligation, that he who made them is able to make them come and do homage.

The petition to have the heart united draws them together as nothing else here does. Clarke gives it the fullest treatment and calls it a most important prayer: it asks that all the purposes, resolutions and affections be joined together, since a divided heart is a great curse and scattered affections are a miserable plague, and when the heart is not at unity with itself the work of religion cannot go on; indecision of mind and division of affection mar any work, and the heart must be one that the work may be one. Ellicott says the same in a sentence, that all the powers are to be concentrated on one service and that an undivided will is equally essential in morals and in religion. John Wesley compresses it to knitting the whole heart to God, and Gill makes the parallel petition ask for further instruction in a way already known. But the last verse divides them sharply. Clarke insists the phrase must mean more than the grave, a place of perdition for the soul as the grave is a place of corruption for the body, and coins the expression a hell below hell. Ellicott denies that any comparison is implied at all, rendering the words as the underworld beneath and arguing from the following verse that what is meant is simply danger of death by violence. Wesley agrees with Ellicott in effect, glossing it as extreme dangers and miseries.
14:
The enemies are read for what their hostility implies. C.H. Spurgeon makes the animus specific — none hate good men so fiercely as the high-minded and domineering, and they hunted in packs, with keen scent and eager foot — and draws from the last clause a general rule: they would not have molested the servant if they had cared a whit for the master, so that those who do not fear God are not afraid to be cruel, an atheist being a misanthrope and irreligion akin to inhumanity. He adds that in persecuting times many a saint has used these words of inquisitors. Adam Clarke puts the same clause as two questions, who sins that sets God before his eyes, and who does not sin that has no consciousness of the divine presence. John Gill reports a Jewish commentator applying the verse to two named persecutors of David. Charles Ellicott observes only that the verse is taken bodily from an earlier psalm.

The answering description of God is admired by two of them for opposite reasons. Spurgeon calls it a truly glorious doxology in which there is not one redundant word, and distributes it: compassion for the weak and sorrowing, grace for the undeserving, longsuffering for the provoking, mercy for the guilty, and truth for the tried; love is one and yet sevenfold, and its white ray contains the whole scale of colours. Clarke goes through the same words in the original, glossing each in turn, and notes that a great many manuscripts read a different divine name at the head of the list. Then he turns to English and finds it wanting: the scanty language of our ancestors, he says, was not adequate to a full rendering of these words, and he quotes two old versions to prove it, one calling God mild and mildhearted and patient and of much mildheartedness and soothfast, the other mercier and merciful and sufferand and of mykel mercy and sothefast, with a note that the first of those words was interpreted as the deed of mercy.

The self-description that follows sets Clarke off on a philological excursion. An older Latin rendering asks God to give his empire to his child, and the old English version follows it with a word for a tender child which the earlier tongue used for a serving man or a male child alike; from that word, Clarke observes, came our knave, which sank to mean an unprincipled servant because so many servants were found to be purloiners of their masters’ property, exactly as the Latin word for thief became the ordinary name for a dishonest one. He supports this with a line from an eclogue asking what the masters will do when the servants dare such things, and with a comic dramatist’s joke that a man is a fellow of three letters, meaning a thief. Clarke also reports that the old paraphrase made the handmaid the church and her son the true believer. On the closing request he and Ellicott converge on the same image: Clarke sees an allusion to the marking of a slave in order to establish whose property he was, and traces our word token to its old root, while Ellicott says the combined expressions of the previous verse imply a homeborn slave. Ellicott adds that the sign asked is one an Israelite saw, and every pious heart still sees, in what to others is an every-day occurrence. Gill notes a reading that referred the token to the kingdom itself.
